::: {.callout-tip}
#### Learning Objectives

- Know how to produce heatmaps of protein abundance data using `pheatmap`, including with correlation-based clustering
- Understand how each argument of `pheatmap` changes a heatmap, and how to plot and interpret a heatmap of any subset of proteins
- Be able to produce a scatter plot comparing log fold changes across two contrasts to identify proteins with shared or specific responses
:::

```{r}
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = here::here("course_files/dia"))
```

```{r}
library("QFeatures")

load("preprocessed/lesson06.rda", verbose = TRUE)
```

Having performed differential abundance analysis, we now want to visualise the results in ways that complement the volcano plots produced in the previous lesson.
In this lesson we produce heatmaps to display protein abundance patterns across all samples simultaneously, and scatter plots to compare fold changes across contrasts to identify proteins with shared or condition-specific responses.

## Heatmaps

::: {.callout-discussion}
#### Discussion

- What are we trying to learn from a heatmap of protein abundances?
  What patterns would you look for?
- Which proteins would you choose to plot --- all quantified proteins, significant proteins, or the most variable?
  What are the trade-offs of each approach?
:::

A heatmap provides a two-dimensional view of protein abundances across all samples simultaneously, and is commonly used alongside hierarchical clustering to reveal groups of proteins and samples with similar abundance patterns.

### Building a heatmap

We build a heatmap of all proteins that were retained after the replication filter in the statistical analysis, adding one feature at a time.

#### The abundance matrix

We extract the quantification matrix and rename the sample columns using the `runCol` column from the `colData`.
We also prepare a data frame of sample annotations that records the group of each sample.

```{r}
#| label: heatmap-abundance-matrix

quant_mtx <- assay(dia_qf[["norm_proteins_replicated"]])

# Rename the samples with their runCol
colnames(quant_mtx) <- dia_qf$runCol

sample_annotations <- colData(dia_qf) %>%
  data.frame() %>%
  tibble::remove_rownames() %>%
  tibble::column_to_rownames('runCol') %>%
  select(group)

head(sample_annotations)
```

#### Plotting the matrix

We first plot the matrix as it is, with the clustering switched off.
Each row is a protein, each column is a sample, and the colour shows the abundance.
Grey cells are missing values.
The rows and columns are in the order of the matrix.

```{r}
#| label: heatmap-unclustered
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-width: 8

pheatmap(
  quant_mtx,
  cluster_rows = FALSE,
  cluster_cols = FALSE,
  show_rownames = FALSE
)
```

The colours mostly reflect how abundant each protein is, so differences between samples are hard to see.

#### Scaling each row

Using `scale = 'row'` standardises each row to mean=0 and sd=1 (Z-score).
This allows us to focus on the relative abundance of each protein across samples rather than on its absolute abundance.

```{r}
#| label: heatmap-row-scaled
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-width: 8

pheatmap(
  quant_mtx,
  cluster_rows = FALSE,
  cluster_cols = FALSE,
  show_rownames = FALSE,
  scale = 'row' # standardise each row to mean=0 and sd=1 (Z-score)
)
```

#### Annotating the samples

We add a column annotation bar to indicate the group of each sample.

```{r}
#| label: heatmap-annotated
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-width: 8

pheatmap(
  quant_mtx,
  cluster_rows = FALSE,
  cluster_cols = FALSE,
  show_rownames = FALSE,
  scale = 'row',
  annotation_col = sample_annotations,
  annotation_names_col = FALSE # hide annotation title
)
```

#### Clustering rows and columns

Hierarchical clustering orders the proteins and the samples so that those with similar abundance patterns are next to each other.
`pheatmap` clusters both rows and columns by default, using Euclidean distance and complete linkage.

```{r}
#| label: heatmap-default-clustering
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-width: 8

pheatmap(
  quant_mtx,
  show_rownames = FALSE,
  scale = 'row',
  annotation_col = sample_annotations,
  annotation_names_col = FALSE
)
```

#### Correlation-based distance and Ward linkage

Euclidean distance can be sensitive to the absolute scale of values.
An alternative is to use 1 minus the Pearson correlation as a distance metric, which focuses on the shape of abundance profiles rather than their absolute values.

We could use `clustering_distance_rows = "correlation"` within `pheatmap`, but this does not handle missing values.
Instead, we calculate the correlation-based distance manually using `cor` with `use = "pairwise.complete.obs"` to handle missing values appropriately.
We also use Ward's minimum variance method (`clustering_method = 'ward.D2'`) for the hierarchical clustering, which tends to produce more compact, evenly-sized clusters than the default complete linkage.

```{r}
#| label: heatmap-correlation-ward
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-width: 8

# Calculate correlation-based distance manually, handling NAs with pairwise complete obs
dist_cols <- as.dist(1 - cor(quant_mtx, use = "pairwise.complete.obs"))
dist_rows <- as.dist(1 - cor(t(quant_mtx), use = "pairwise.complete.obs"))

pheatmap(
  quant_mtx,
  show_rownames = FALSE,
  scale = 'row',
  annotation_col = sample_annotations,
  annotation_names_col = FALSE,
  clustering_method = 'ward.D2', # Use Ward's method for hierarchical clustering
  clustering_distance_rows = dist_rows,
  clustering_distance_cols = dist_cols
)
```

#### Colours and layout

Finally, we use a diverging colour palette, which suits Z-scores centred on zero, and adjust the size of the dendrograms and cells.

```{r}
#| label: heatmap-final
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-width: 8

pheatmap(
  quant_mtx,
  scale = 'row',
  show_rownames = FALSE,
  annotation_col = sample_annotations,
  clustering_method = 'ward.D2',
  clustering_distance_rows = dist_rows,
  clustering_distance_cols = dist_cols,
  color = colorRampPalette(brewer.pal(n = 7, name = "RdBu"))(100), # Use a diverging color palette
  annotation_names_col = FALSE,
  treeheight_row = 100, # default is 50 — increase to give row dendrogram more space
  treeheight_col = 100, # default is 50 — increase to give col dendrogram more space
  cellwidth = 10, # fix cell width in points
  cellheight = 0.25
)
```

::: {.callout-exercise}
#### Challenge: Heatmaps of protein subsets

{{< level 2 >}}

Plotting every protein can make it difficult to see structure.
Choose a subset of the replicated proteins and plot a heatmap of it, using the code above as a template.
You could use, for example:

- Proteins with a significant overall difference across groups according to the F-test (`adj.P.Val < 0.05`)
- Proteins significant (`adj.P.Val < 0.05`) in at least one pairwise contrast
- Proteins significant in one contrast only

For your heatmap, consider:

- How do the proteins and samples cluster?
- Do the sample groups separate cleanly?
- How does the choice of subset change what the heatmap can show?

<details><summary>Hint</summary>The row names of `quant_mtx` are UniProt IDs, so you can select rows with a vector of IDs taken from `limma_results_F` or `limma_results_all_contrasts`.
Calculate the row and column distances again for the subset before passing them to `pheatmap`.</details>

::::: {.callout-answer collapse="true"}
This example uses the proteins with a significant overall difference across groups according to the F-test.

```{r}
#| label: heatmap-f-test-proteins
#| fig-height: 10
#| fig-width: 10

sig_prot_F <- limma_results_F %>%
  filter(adj.P.Val < 0.05) %>%
  pull(UniprotID)

subset_mtx <- quant_mtx[sig_prot_F, ]

# Use concatenation of gene name and UniprotID as row label
rownames(subset_mtx) <- sprintf(
  '%s (%s)',
  rowData(dia_qf[["norm_proteins_replicated"]])[sig_prot_F, "Genes"],
  sig_prot_F
)

dist_cols_subset <- as.dist(1 - cor(subset_mtx, use = "pairwise.complete.obs"))
dist_rows_subset <- as.dist(1 - cor(t(subset_mtx), use = "pairwise.complete.obs"))

pheatmap(
  subset_mtx,
  scale = 'row',
  annotation_col = sample_annotations,
  annotation_names_col = FALSE,
  clustering_method = 'ward.D2',
  clustering_distance_rows = dist_rows_subset,
  clustering_distance_cols = dist_cols_subset,
  color = colorRampPalette(brewer.pal(n = 7, name = "RdBu"))(100),
  fontsize = 8
)
```

The control samples cluster together and apart from most of the infected samples, while the MPXV and COVID-19 samples are less clearly separated from each other.

The proteins were selected because they differ between the groups, so the groups separate more clearly than they would for a random set of proteins.
A heatmap of the significant proteins therefore illustrates the result of the test rather than providing independent evidence for it.
A heatmap of all proteins shows the dominant structure in the whole data set, including patterns unrelated to the groups.
:::::
:::

## Comparing log fold changes across contrasts

A scatter plot of log fold changes from two contrasts --- here MPXV vs Control and COVID-19 vs Control --- is one way to visualise to what extent the response to both infections is shared or infection-specific.

We first use `pivot_wider` to reshape the results so that each protein occupies a single row, with separate columns for the log fold change and adjusted p-value from each contrast.

```{r}
#| label: extract-genes-below-threshold
compare_limma_results <- limma_results_all_contrasts %>%
  select(UniprotID, Genes, adj.P.Val, logFC, contrast) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = contrast, values_from = c(adj.P.Val, logFC))
```

We can now plot the log fold changes against each other.

```{r}
#| label: scatter-fold-changes
compare_limma_results %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = logFC_MPXV_control, y = logFC_Covid19_control)) +
  geom_point() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    x = "Log Fold Change (MPXV vs Control)",
    y = "Log Fold Change (COVID-19 vs Control)"
  )
```

::: {.callout-discussion}
#### Discussion

The plot shows one point per protein and nothing else.

- What other information would help us interpret it?
- Which of that information do we already have in `compare_limma_results` or in the earlier analysis, and which would we need to calculate?
- How could each addition be shown: a colour, a point size, a label, a reference line?
:::

We'd like to highlight the significance status of each protein across the two contrasts.
We can create a `sig` column that categorises each protein by its significance status across the two contrasts, distinguishing proteins significant in both, in only one, or in neither.

```{r}
#| label: create-complex-scatter
compare_limma_results <- compare_limma_results %>%
  mutate(
    sig = case_when(
      adj.P.Val_MPXV_control < 0.05 & adj.P.Val_Covid19_control < 0.05 ~ "Both",
      adj.P.Val_MPXV_control < 0.05 &
        adj.P.Val_Covid19_control >= 0.05 ~ "MPXV only",
      adj.P.Val_MPXV_control >= 0.05 &
        adj.P.Val_Covid19_control < 0.05 ~ "COVID-19 only",
      TRUE ~ "None"
    )
  )
```

Now we can re-plot the log fold changes against each other, colouring points by significance category.
We will label only those significant in both contrasts to keep the plot legible.

```{r}
#| label: combine-plots-grid
p <- compare_limma_results %>%
  arrange(desc(sig)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = logFC_MPXV_control, y = logFC_Covid19_control)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = sig), pch = 20, size = 3) +
  geom_text_repel(
    data = filter(compare_limma_results, sig == "Both"),
    aes(label = Genes),
    size = 3,
    colour = 'grey20',
    max.overlaps = 100
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    x = "Log Fold Change (MPXV vs Control)",
    y = "Log Fold Change (COVID-19 vs Control)"
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(
      "Both" = "purple",
      "MPXV only" = "orangered4",
      "COVID-19 only" = "steelblue",
      "None" = "grey70"
    )
  )

print(p)
```

Finally, we map transparency (`alpha`) to the significance category to draw the eye towards proteins significant in both contrasts, and add a linear regression line with `geom_smooth(method = 'lm')` to show the overall relationship between log fold changes across the two infections.

```{r}
#| label: combined-figure-publication
p2 <- p +
  aes(alpha = sig) +
  scale_alpha_manual(
    values = c(
      "Both" = 0.8,
      "MPXV only" = 0.8,
      "COVID-19 only" = 0.8,
      "None" = 0.25
    )
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    aes(x = logFC_MPXV_control, y = logFC_Covid19_control),
    inherit.aes = FALSE, # Don't inherit aesthetics to avoid inheriting alpha aesthetics
    method = 'lm',
    se = FALSE,
    linetype = 2,
    colour = 'grey'
  ) +
  theme(legend.title = element_blank())

print(p2)
```

::: {.callout-discussion}
#### Discussion

- What are we trying to learn from this scatter plot --- what does a protein's position in the plot tell us?
- Which proteins are most interesting?
- The plot includes a linear regression line.
  Is a standard linear model (Ordinary Least Squares; OLS) appropriate here, given that both axes represent quantities measured with error?
  What would be a better alternative?
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
#### Key Points

- Heatmaps are a useful way to visualise protein abundance patterns across all samples simultaneously; restricting to a subset of proteins makes them easier to interpret
- The default Euclidean distance metric in `pheatmap` can be replaced with a correlation-based distance to focus clustering on the shape of abundance profiles; this requires computing the distance matrix manually when missing values are present
- Ward's minimum variance linkage (`clustering_method = 'ward.D2'`) tends to produce more compact, evenly-sized clusters than the default complete linkage
- Building a heatmap one argument at a time (row scaling, sample annotation, clustering, colours) shows what each contributes
- The choice of protein subset determines what a heatmap can show; a heatmap of proteins selected for differing between groups will separate those groups by construction
- Scatter plots of log fold changes from two contrasts can reveal proteins with shared or condition-specific responses; reshaping results to wide format with `pivot_wider` is a convenient way to align values from different contrasts for comparison
:::
